title: A Rude and Necessary Awakening: What a Recent FTC Amicus Brief Means for EdTech and What Parents and Schools Need to Know
author: Emily Cherkin
summary: Emily Cherkin explains the August 2025 FTC amicus brief in the IXL COPPA class action and why it matters for schools using ed-tech with children under 13. Her central claim is that the long-assumed theory of school consent, where a school stands in for parents, is not in the law, and companies must obtain actual informed parental consent. She walks through what COPPA is, how it applies at school, and what the brief says. She then turns to practice: check-a-box forms will no longer suffice, schools cannot compel consent, and schools may act only as an intermediary passing on parents actual consent. She warns that schools failing to adapt face legal and contractual risk, and urges parents to share the brief with their schools.
points: The brief says school consent is not and never has been the law, so COPPA requires actual informed parental consent for ed-tech data collection.
COPPA has no school carve-out, so it applies equally to an app used at school or at home.
Schools may relay parents consent to vendors but cannot substitute their own, nor force parents to agree.
Schools that rely on blanket consent forms face litigation and breach-of-contract exposure if vendors expect them to collect consent.
quotes: Parents are also often expected to acknowledge that their child’s misuse of the device will be the parent’s responsibility, should the device get damaged or broken.

And up until last week’s filing, many EdTech companies have sought permission only from schools–and not from parents, as COPPA requires–as to what information is collected about students and how that information may be commercialized.
COPPA does not include any carve outs with respect to internet platforms that are used at school. This means that COPPA applies with equal force whether a child is using an app at school or at home.
This amicus brief establishes that schools can no longer stand in the shoes of parents for the purpose of consenting to data collection.
Significantly, this means that EdTech companies must now ensure that they have informed consent from a child’s parent, and that those “check a box” forms will no longer suffice.
Schools are not authorized to substitute their own consent for that of parents.
